Систем

Alternative forms

  • (the United States of America): Merica/ 'Murica/ 'murica (nonstandard, often jocular or representing dialect)
  • (North and South America): Americas

Етимологија {{{2}}}|

    Етимолошко стабло
    New Latin Americalbor.
    Енглески America

    Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q1248221 site=enwiki, feminine Latinized form of the Italian first name of Amerigo Vespucci (1454–1512). Amerigo is an Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates/derived: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q652 site=enwiki name derived from a Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates/derived: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q21200 site=enwiki language and is etymologically related to Henry and Emmerich. The earliest known use of America for the (South) American continent is on a 1507 map by Martin Waldseemüller;[1][2] see Naming of the Americas for more.

    Although this is the most widely accepted derivation, it has also been suggested that it could originate from the name of the Amerrisque mountains in Nicaragua (from Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates/derived: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q33738 site=enwiki), and another disputed theory is that it derives from the surname of Richard Amerike (1440–1503), whose surname is an anglicised form of Welsh ap Meurig (“son of Meurig”), from Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates/derived: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q2266723 site=enwiki, which could be a rendition of Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates/cognate: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q397 site=enwiki (compare Maurice).[3]

        The results of my examination ... for the most part allied to plants of the cooler part of America, or the uplands of the tropical latitudes ...
      • 1890, Encyclopaedia Britannica, page 796:
        the Marsupials or pouched animals, being found throughout the continent of America, from the United States to Patagonia

        Franciscan attitudes in the Canaries offered possible precedents for what Europe now came to call ‘the New World’, or, through a somewhat tangled chain of circumstances, ‘America’.
    2. Lua error in Модул:names: Unrecognized gender: female.
    3. Lua error in Модул:place: IndexType.
    4. Lua error in Модул:senseid/templates: Wikibase entity snapshot missing entity=Q30 The United States of America.

        For a long time the dormouse and polecat had seemed to him overfeeble enemies for his restless valour, even as the granary floor seemed to afford too narrow a field. Every day he read the papers of the previous day in the servants' hall of the houses he visited, and it appeared to him that this war in America, which was hailed as the awakening of the spirit of liberty and justice in the New World, ought to produce a revolution in France.
      • 2013 мај 25, “No hiding place”, in The Economist‎[6], volume 407, page 74:
        In America alone, people spent $170 billion on “direct marketing”—junk mail of both the physical and electronic varieties—last year. Yet of those who received unsolicited adverts through the post, only 3% bought anything as a result.
      • 2014 јул 27, “Nuclear Weapons”, in Last Week Tonight with John Oliver, season 1, episode 12, John Oliver (actor), via HBO:

      • 2022 April 3, Roisin Conaty & al., Big Fat Quiz of Everything, Channel 4:
        Captain America, how did he get his powers?
        I think he... he got bitten by America.

    Usage notes

    In English, the unqualified term "America" often refers to the United States of America as a synecdoche, with "American" typically referring to people and things from that country. The sense of "the Americas" varies in commonness between regions in contemporary English, but is found in certain circumstances, such as in reference to the Organization of American States.

    Латински

    Етимологија {{{2}}}|

      Feminine form of Americus, the Latinized form of the forename of Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci (1454–1512). Amerigo is the Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates/derived: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q652 site=enwiki form of a Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates/derived: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q21200 site=enwiki personal name (see Emmerich).

      First recorded in 1507 (together with the related term Amerigen) in the Cosmographiae Introductio, apparently written by Matthias Ringmann, in reference to South America;[1] first applied to both North and South America by Mercator in 1538. Amerigen means "land of Amerigo" and derives from Amerigo and gen, the accusative case of Greek gē "earth". America accorded with the feminine names of Asia, Africa, and Europa.[2]

      Pronunciation

      • () МФА(кључ): /a.meˈriː.ka/, [ämɛˈriːkä] or МФА(кључ): /aˈme.ri.ka/, [äˈmɛrɪkä]
      • () МФА(кључ): /a.meˈri.ka/, [ämeˈriːkä] or МФА(кључ): /aˈme.ri.ka/, [äˈmɛːrikä]
      • Note: the length of the /i/ can be long, and that form is well-attested in Latin literature; for example, Rafael Landívar's Rusticatio Mexicana. This form is mostly attested in poetry, and it corresponds more closely to the Italian pronunciation of Amerigo.[3]

      1. (New Latin) America (the continent).

      [[Категорија:Латински terms derived from Италијански|AMERICA]] Feminine form of ''Americus'', the Latinized form of the forename of Italian explorer [[:w:Amerigo Vespucci|Amerigo Vespucci]] (1454–1512). [[Amerigo#Италијански|Amerigo]] is the Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates/derived: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q652 site=enwiki form of a Lua error in Модул:etymology/templates/derived: Wikibase sitelink snapshot missing entity=Q21200 site=enwiki personal name (see [[Emmerich#Енглески|Emmerich]]). First recorded in 1507 (together with the related term ''Amerigen'') in the ''[[w:Cosmographiae Introductio|Cosmographiae Introductio]]'', apparently written by [[w:Matthias Ringmann|Matthias Ringmann]], in reference to South America;John R. Hebert, "The Map That Named America: Library Acquires 1507 Waldseemüller Map of the World" ([http://www.loc.gov/loc/lcib/0309/maps.html]), ''Information Bulletin'', Library of Congress first applied to both North and South America by Mercator in 1538. ''Amerigen'' means "land of Amerigo" and derives from ''Amerigo'' and ''[[gen]]'', the accusative case of Greek ''[[γῆ|gē]]'' "earth".
